newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to offer glimpse of euro's role on global stage.
newsitem.headline: EU to offer glimpse of euro's role on global stage.

text.p: A single European currency will pose a strong threat to the dollar's market dominance but transition to a bipolar monetary system is likely to happen only gradually, European Union sources said.

This view is likely to emerge in a report due on Wednesday from the European Commission, the first official EU attempt to assess the broader implications of economic and monetary union (EMU), they said.
In view of the dollar's dominance across a broad spectrum of markets and initial uncertainty over the euro's credibility, the U.S. currency's influence is expected to be eroded only gradually.

Although the dollar's use as a reserve currency has declined in recent years -- 63 percent of official reserves were held in dollars in 1994 compared with 76 percent in 1973 -- it is still by far the most dominant currency traded on foreign exchange markets.
The dollar is involved in 83 percent of global foreign exchange transactions, with a strong role in swaps and futures markets and in Asia.
This last point is seen as critical by the Commission, one that is likely keep a new global regime from becoming a tripolar system, with the yen rounding out the group.

For example, recent figures show that close to 48 percent of Japanese exports and 75 percent of imports are priced in dollars. The U.S. currency's strong role in Asia also extends to the financial centres of Hong Kong and Singapore.
Adding to its pre-eminence is its widespread use among the emerging economies of Latin America.
The euro is likely to have a competitive edge as an anchor currency for the European continent -- including central and eastern Europe -- the Mediterranean and several African Sub-Saharan countries.
"(The euro) is bound to become the anchor for central Europe since these countries want to be members of the EU," said one EU official.
Among the other issues that may be addressed in the report is the effect that portfolio diversification will play in determining whether the euro gets off to a quick start.
On this front, there are conflicting views.

One sees the euro taking some of the shine off the dollar's role as a safe-haven currency. Another positive factor is the potential for a euro-denominated debt market to cause a shift of assets out of U.S. and Asian capital markets.

If all EU countries eventually join EMU, the resulting bond market would become the largest in world with an aggregate market capitalisation approaching $1,000 billion above that of the U.S. Treasury market, say analysts at Goldman Sachs.

The euro could also benefit from a shift in the current imbalance in trade invoicing. Although the United States accounts for only 12 percent of world trade, roughly 48 percent is invoiced in dollars.
The situation could be radically altered with the introduction of a single European currency since the EU accounts for about 38 percent of world exports and imports.

On the other hand, EMU would not allow for the same degree of portfolio diversification as at present in Europe. This might cause investors to place some of their funds outside the euro area, analysts said.
